clue.text: Perhaps Freud regularly haggled for a reduction

parts.note: Freud was a psychoanalyst, and a shrink is slang for one; 'Perhaps' marks him as an example

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so only every other letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Sigmund Freud bargaining hard to get money knocked off the price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps Freud' points to the slang word for a psychiatrist, not to anything Freudian.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrinkage is the amount by which something gets smaller, so it is a decrease or cut.

clue.text: Philosopher somewhat impervious to iconoclasm

indicators.note: somewhat means only a part, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A thinker who is unmoved by people smashing sacred images.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: a Stoic is famously impervious to upset.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stoic is a follower of the ancient Greek school founded by Zeno, so a kind of philosopher.

clue.text: Repeat of complex rite before the queen dined

indicators.note: complex means intricate or tangled, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: An elaborate ceremony staged again before the queen sat down to dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: To reiterate is to say or do something again, a direct synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Wild Thing and hits in discos

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of the next word run riot into a new order

parts.note: to club is to hit, so hits is clubs

explanation.surface: The song Wild Thing and other chart hits playing in dance halls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild Thing' reads as the Troggs' song title, but Wild is the anagram signal and hits is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Discos are venues for dancing to recorded music, which is what nightclubs are.

clue.text: Part of a chair Starmer's broken

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces that can be put back in a different order

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, has broken a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is the UK Prime Minister; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An armrest is the side support of a seat on which the sitter's arm lies, a component of the seat.

clue.text: Illegal drug simple to swallow around street

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so the next letters go into the middle of the word for simple

parts.note: c. (circa) means around, as in dates

explanation.surface: A banned pill that is simple to swallow, bought around the street.
explanation.walkthrough: The circa abbreviation and the street abbreviation sit together inside the word for simple.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstasy is the street name of MDMA, a controlled recreational substance.

clue.text: Tweet of little value, we hear

indicators.note: hearing points to how a word is pronounced rather than spelt

explanation.surface: A social media post that is of little worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tweet' suggests social media, but it is the call of a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheep is the short high call of a young bird, as is a tweet.

clue.text: Tea time discussion

parts.note: char or cha is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A natter over a cuppa at teatime.
explanation.definitionFit: A chat is an informal conversation, a light talk between people.

clue.text: Duck of a crimson colour that is from the south

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading from the south means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: crimson is a shade of red

explanation.surface: Describing a duck whose plumage is a deep crimson.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large northern sea duck prized for its soft down feathers.

clue.text: E.g. Bonnie Prince Charlie in power, concerned with money

parts.note: P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: The Jacobite prince once in power and worried about his finances.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonnie Prince Charlie, Charles Edward Stuart, led the 1745 rising to claim the British throne.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretender is a claimant to a throne he does not hold; Charles Stuart was known as the Young Pretender.

clue.text: Having debts, now criminal receives one grand

indicators.note: criminal means crooked, so the letters of the preceding word are bent into a new order
receiving means taking something in, so a letter goes inside the rearranged word

parts.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: Someone in debt, now that a crook has been handed a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Owing describes a person who still has to pay money back, in debt to someone.

clue.text: Mess up in skirmish and leave

indicators.note: in says the letters are found inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Botching things during a fight and then walking away.
explanation.definitionFit: To mishandle something is to manage it badly, to botch or bungle it.

clue.text: Make conversation as Mrs Sprat did

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an idiom for chatting idly
second meaning, read literally: the nursery-rhyme wife who could eat no lean meat

explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, Jack Sprat could eat no fat and his wife could eat no lean, so she ate the fatty parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to gossip or talk at leisure; literally it describes eating fatty meat.

clue.text: Complimentary about iron covers

indicators.note: covering something means going around it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A gift related to an iron with protective covers.
explanation.definitionFit: Complimentary items are given without charge, at no cost.

clue.text: Ignoring endings, cast able and can film

indicators.note: to ignore the endings is to drop the final letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: A capable cast and a can of footage: the makings of a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Each of the four words loses its last letter and the remains run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Casablanca is the 1942 Bogart and Bergman movie, a famous example of cinema.

clue.text: It's a bright colour, little bit of skin damage?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, whimsical: a small scar, with the diminutive ending -let as in piglet

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is invented: just as a piglet is a little pig, a tiny scar would be a scar-let.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlet is a brilliant red hue, and split up it reads as a diminutive of a mark left by a wound.

clue.text: Ocean views, for instance within south-eastern headlands

indicators.note: within means inside, so the short word sits between the two pieces that follow

parts.note: as in 'such as', introducing an example

explanation.surface: Coastal vistas, for example from promontories in the south-east.
explanation.definitionFit: Seascapes are pictures or vistas of the sea, so marine views.

clue.text: Wished company finally made money

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: to earn is to make money

explanation.surface: A firm that hoped it would finally turn a profit.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long for something, so yearned means longed or desired.

clue.text: Designed logos? Mine shows new word

indicators.note: something designed is made up or arranged afresh, so the letters are laid out in a new order

explanation.surface: A graphic designer proudly presenting company emblems they created.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologism is a freshly coined term or expression not yet established in the language.

clue.text: Excellent beer emptied and knocked back — one cold bitter

indicators.note: knocked back means turned back, so the remaining letters are read in the opposite direction
emptying a word removes its contents, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: C for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A great ale downed in one, followed by a chilled bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' and 'bitter' both suggest drinking, but bitter here is the adjective meaning sharp-tongued.
explanation.definitionFit: Acerbic means sharp and harsh in tone or taste, close in sense to biting or sour.

clue.text: Colouring materials beginning to colour synthetic fabrics

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Starting to dye artificial textiles with a set of colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Crayons are sticks of coloured wax or chalk used for drawing, art supplies.

clue.text: Charm heartless girl with love for the French

indicators.note: without a heart, the middle of the word is gone and only its ends survive

explanation.surface: A cold-hearted girl who still charms with her French idea of love.
explanation.definitionFit: Glamour is alluring attractiveness or allure, much like charm as a noun.

clue.text: Skimpy underwear item is a bit of a fiddle

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a minimal pair of briefs
second meaning: one of the four strings of a violin

explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a fiddle' suggests a swindle or a fiddly job; here a fiddle is a violin and the bit is one of its strings.
explanation.definitionFit: The name covers both scanty undergarment and the lowest string on a violin, tuned to the note G.

clue.text: Commanding officer with case for detective Morse?

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outside letters of the next word are kept

explanation.surface: An officer brought in on a case for Inspector Morse, the TV detective.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a British TV detective, which makes 'detective Morse' look like one unit; the question mark flags Morse as an example of a signalling system.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse is a signalling system of dots and dashes standing for letters, an instance of a cipher system.

clue.text: E.g. hummus and salsa on bagel for toper

parts.note: a bagel is ring-shaped, like the letter

explanation.surface: Spreading party dips on a bagel to feed a heavy drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is a habitual drinker, and dipso is slang short for dipsomaniac, an alcoholic.

clue.text: Groups of soldiers cricketer cheers with pride?

parts.note: ta is British slang for thanks
a pride is a group of lions; the question mark flags the indirect route

explanation.surface: A batsman cheered on with pride by his team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' reads as a feeling, but it is the collective noun for big cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Battalions are large army units made up of several companies of troops.

clue.text: Actor Charlie, son of Martin, spotted astride horse

indicators.note: straddling something puts a leg either side of it, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: H is slang for heroin, known as horse

explanation.surface: The actor Charlie Sheen spotted riding a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is a slang name for heroin, abbreviated H.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Sheen is the American actor, son of the actor Martin Sheen.

clue.text: Bank really giving away a pound

indicators.note: giving something away means losing it, so letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: L for pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A bank actually handing out a pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like a noun, but it is the verb, as in 'bank on'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on something is to count on or depend upon it.

clue.text: City coach, one carrying Evita's spicy food

parts.note: Pep Guardiola manages Manchester City football club
Evita was Eva Perón of Argentina

explanation.surface: A football manager carrying something belonging to Eva Perón, the Argentine first lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepperoni is a spicy Italian-American dry salami, the classic pizza topping.

clue.text: Sound made by hooter drawing one in

indicators.note: drawing something in pulls it inside, so a letter goes into the word for hooter
in completes the phrase about drawing, placing the letter inside

explanation.surface: The racket a car horn makes when someone sketches it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooter' suggests a horn that makes a sound; it is slang for the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Noise is any sound, especially a loud or unwanted one.

clue.text: Fib from Sunak originally, and one from his party

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so the first letter of the name is taken

parts.note: Rishi Sunak led the Conservatives, whose members are Tories

explanation.surface: A lie told first by Rishi Sunak and then by another Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak is a former UK Prime Minister from the Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A story, in informal use, is a lie or untruth, as in 'don't tell stories'.

clue.text: Worker who's on track maligns rewritten article

indicators.note: rewriting a word lets its letters be set down again in another order

explanation.surface: A staffer who keeps on track while rewriting a defamatory article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On track' sounds like 'doing well', but means on the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A signalman operates the signals on a railway line, so his job is literally beside the rails.
